This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 384 columns across 28 data files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 28 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

PubPeer Comments

We checked 33 references with DOIs. No references with comments in PubPeer were found.

RetractionWatch

We checked 33 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the RetractionWatch database were found.

Replication Check

We checked 33 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the FLoRA database were found.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Research on the imagination has examined how changing the contents and spatial framing of a mental scenes changes that scene. But hardly any work has changing the temporal reference frame of the imagination. For an ideal simulator, changing the frame-rate in which something is imagined should not matter for scene content, but it is unknown whether changing the temporal frame affects people's imagination. Across three studies and six experiments (N = 223 after exclusions), participants watched stylized and naturalistic scenarios of projectile and pendulum motion at different playback speeds, and continued them in their mind. Our set-up dissociates temporal reference frame from content speed, which allowed us to compare people's predictions to simulation models that do or don't separate content from temporal frame. We found that participants could adjust their imagined temporal reference. Participants also kept content separate from reference-frame speed in realistic (but not stylized) scenes.

[div-01]

Suppose you're watching a game of soccer on television. You see a ball kicked full force towards the goal, the goalie diving just in time to make the save. The dramatic moment is then replayed in slow motion.

The goal-keeper now seems to float like an unhurried blimp towards the ball, as it drifts slowly to the goal.

Despite the change in visible motion, you're under no illusion that gravity has changed, or that the ball will hit the goalie with any less force. But now consider: when you imagine something happening in slow-motion (like a ball moving slowly towards a face), do you actually disentangle the internal and external dynamics of the imagined this? Does a ball moving in slow-motion in the mind move less far? Any mental scene is made up of content (objects, characters, events, properties, and so on) and reference frames (spatial and temporal). These two components, content and reference frame, can vary independently.

To go back to our opening example, you might imagine different players taking different shots in a soccer game. This would be a change of the contents of your mental scene. You could also imagine the exact same An example of an everyday scene unfolding at normal playback speed (1×). One could either change the content speed, e.g. making the player and ball genuinely move faster, so that the ball travels farther in the same scene time. Or, one could change the reference-frame speed, e.g. making the whole scene play at 2×, so events occur sooner relative to an external clock, but object velocities are unchanged. (b) The paradigm we used in our studies dissociate content properties and reference frame by using motion types that map changes in either content or reference frame to different judgements. Here, we show the example of projectile motion, specifically a cart rolling off a cliff. Increasing the horizontal cart speed will make it fall further, but not change its vertical speed, and so not change the time to impact. Making the entire scene run faster will make the cart hit the ground sooner (relative to an external clock), but not change where it ends up. So, having participants judge 'where' the cart ended up and 'when' it hit the ground allows us to work backwards to how they reason when speeding up or slowing down a mental scene.

shot happening from multiple angles. This would be a change of spatial reference frame or perspective.

Importantly for us here, you could also vary the temporal reference frame of your imagination (see Fig. 24 1a). That is, you could imagine a player truly moving more slowly or quickly towards the ball (a change in 25 content speed), or you could imagine the entire scene is unfolding more slowly or more quickly (a change While extensive previous research has examined how changes in spatial reference affect the imagination, hardly any work has examined whether and how changes in temporal reference affect the contents of the imagination. Here, we asked: can the mind represent a change in reference-frame speed independent of a change in content speed? That is: does speeding up or slowing down a mental simulation affect the contents of the mental simulation itself?

To address this question, we adopt an approach based on the notion that the mind can reason about the dynamics of everyday objects by running a kind of simplified, internal world model [1] [2] [3] [4] . On this approach, the mind runs a mental simulation that is akin to the simulations developed by engineers to capture simplified versions of the real world that run in approximately real time (for either scientific or entertainment purposes).

This approach has support from computational, behavioral, and neurological studies 5 , but it also has its alternatives and critiques [6] [7] [8] [9] . Overall there appears to be a growing consensus that the mind is likely using different computations (or combining them) to solve different aspects of intuitive physics [10] [11] [12] , and that even if the mind does use mental simulation, then simulation must use a variety of principled approximations and workarounds 3, 13, 14.

Two main possibilities seem a priori possible: On one hand, the mind's mental simulation might work like an actual simulation, in which case speeding up or slowing down the reference-frame speed should not affect the content. Hitting 'fast forward' on a video might make a player seem to move faster, but the ball they kick will not travel any further. Events also appear faster relative to an external clock, not an internal one. On the other hand, it is possible that the mind cannot disentangle inner and external clocks. This may be because the mind does not start by establishing certain properties of the scene prior to generating a mental image, but rather 'reads off' those properties from the scene, including properties such as force and velocity, which in turn affect the next predicted image. This may also come about because of resource limitations: pushing a computer game to run faster requires greater resources and so may result in loss of fidelity for aspects of the scene. Beyond these two options, it is also possible for behavior to be mixed and nuanced, such that people will be better at separating reference-frame speed and content speed in some scenes, and not others. The different options are not something that is immediately distinguished by introspection: we encourage the reader to try for themselves to imagine a person throwing a ball in double-time, and try to assess where the ball will end up or how hard it will hit a wall.

Previous research has examined related, but separate questions. The separation between imagined content and reference frame has been extensively examined in spatial reference frames. There is a vast literature on this topic, but for our purposes it is sufficient to note that a great deal of research has studied questions related to changing spatial frames in the imagination, including the use of allocentric vs. egocentric reference frames in memory, navigation, and imagination 15 , the adoption of different points of view on the same scene 16, 17 , the different functions and levels of abstraction associated with different spatial perspectives 18, 19 , the cognitive neuroscience parallels of different mental perspectives on a scene 20 , the development of perspective taking 21, 22 , and so on. At the risk of over-simplification, this research has generally found that changes to spatial reference can induce changes to the contents of mental simulation and their processing, and that different spatial references are associated with different functions, neural implementations, and developmental timelines. By comparison to this line of work, much less work has examined the effect of changes in temporal reference frames on the imagination.

Beyond spatial frames, past work on the imagination has also studied the internal timing over which events unfold. Experiments on mental transformations (such as rotation or translation) and mental scanning have found striking correspondence between the time that it would take to carry out such operations in reality, and the time that it takes to imagine them [23] [24] [25] [26] . While this research has examined the speed of mental simulation, it did not examine the effects of asking participants to imagine scenes as happening in a faster or slower frame. Research on the mental simulation of actions, movement, and motor imagery has also found a correspondence between the external timing and complexity of a given motion, and the time it takes to imagine this motion 27, 28 . This line of research sometimes asks people to imagine the action happening faster or slower 29 , but that question does not separate content speed (the action actually happening faster or slower) from reference-frame speed (the scene as a whole unfolding in slow motion or fast-forward).

Another related-but-separate area of research is the phenomenon of mental replay. Previous work that studied human and non-human navigation, episodic memory, and the imagination of past and future events has found that replay of structured events happens in a compressed format [30] [31] [32] . That is, when people or nonhuman animals recall past episodes or paths (or run them forward), it appears that these events happen on a compressed timescale relative to their real-world counterparts. Some early research took this compressed timescale to suggest that the (re)imagined events are played in an accelerated frame, like watching a video in fast-forward. More recent research suggests that the compression is due to the replay's focus on the important moments of interest, more akin to watching snapshots or highlights of an event, which takes less time than watching the entire event again 33 . We do not mean to take up the question of what compression in replay represents, and only note that whatever the case, these studies do not focus on whether a directed change in mental frame rate affects the contents of the imagined scene.

Here, we examined whether the mind can represent a distortion in reference-frame speed independent of the content speed, and adjust mental simulation accordingly. Across three studies and six experiments, participants viewed clips with different playback speeds of projectile motion (Study 1: animated scenes; Study 2: naturalistic scenes) or pendulum motion (Study 3). Participants were asked to mentally simulate how events would continue to unfold, and judged when and where certain events would take place. Our choice of stimuli was set up in advance such that the judgement of when an event happened tracked changes to reference-frame speed, while where an event happened tracked changes to content speed. As we explain further in the methods, this mapping is not some universal feature of changes to mental simulation, but rather a generalizable and useful experimental design choice. This separation also allows us to construct different mental simulation models that either do or do not take into account changes in reference frame, and then do or do not correctly use those to mentally simulate the contents of a scene.

To briefly summarize our results up front, we found that across all three studies the judgements of event timing varied with the playback speed. This is expected, but important to establish, and it suggests that people do indeed take into account frame rate changes in their mental simulation. In other words, a video shown in slow motion (or sped up) will be imagined as continuing in slow motion (or sped up). Beyond this, we found that in animated scenes (Study 1), position judgements also varied with the playback speed, which suggests that in these scenes the content is affected by reference changes. However, in the realistic scenes (Study 2 and 3), position judgements align with a model that distinctly represents frame-rate and content speed. Taken altogether, our results suggest that (i) the mind can unfold scenes in sped-up or slowed-down frames, and (ii) this change in reference frame can have an effect on less familiar, stylized situations, but (iii) for realistic situations the mind is closer to an accurate simulation that does not actually change the properties of objects with the frame rate. After detailing our results and models, we consider the possible reasons for, and implications of our findings, as well as future directions for the study of different temporal frames in the imagination.

1 General Methods

1.1 Participants

All studies were conducted online 34 , recruiting US-based participants via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co.

co).

The experiments themselves were coded in jsPsych, and hosted on our lab server. Participants were compensated for their time at a rate of 12 USD per hour. The studies were approved under IRB19-1861 (Commonsense Reasoning in Physics and Psychology). All participants provided informed consent. All stimuli involved either video animations, videos of simple real scenes, or still images that were created using Python, Keynote, or iMovie. All data and stimuli are available at the following repository: https://osf.io/e3yzh/overview?view_only=7f7b7566e6d54983b8079345f89f3243. You can try all experiments at https://cocodev.opalstacked.com/experiments/hanbei/einstein_experiment/demo_page/einstein_project_demo_page.html. All studies, including experimental procedures, number of participants, exclusion criteria, and analyses, were pre-registered https://osf.io/wyxag/overview?view_only=5efb1352ba2743b3ba7d36be3f368dce. Data for the main studies was collected on October 6, 2026.

In each experiment, we recruited 40 participants. Sample sizes were determined on the basis of pilot studies, which were then used for a bootstrap analysis, indicating that 40 participants per experiment provide greater than 95% power to distinguish the hypotheses.

1.2 Mental simulation models

Across the experiments, we compared four possible mental simulation models, that differed in terms of how they took into account changes in reference-frame speed and content speed. It is easiest to understand the differences between these models with reference to a simple example (see also Fig. 1b), which also parallels the stimuli for Studies 1 and 2. Consider a toy cart moving horizontally from left to right along a table that is h = 1 meter in height. The cart moves at a horizontal speed of v = 10 meters/second. When the cart reaches the end of the table, it falls off. Using basic Newtonian physics we know the time till the cart hits the ground is t = √︂ 2h g , and the horizontal distance that the cart will cover after it goes over the edge of the table is d = v•t. Approximating g = 9.8 m s 2 , we get that the cart will take 0.45 seconds to hit the ground, and it will hit the ground 4.5 meters to the right of the edge of the table. Next, suppose that all of this was initially filmed at a standard frame rate f . This frame-rate could correspond to, say, 24 frames a second. To make the following discussion and expressions easier, we can arbitrarily take the standard frame rate to be f = 1.

And lastly, suppose that the original video is now instead shown playing at double time, f ′ = 2 • f (this is why we set f = 1, so all that matters is the ratio between the new frame rate and the standard one). So, the perceived speed of the cart will appear to an outside viewer to be v ′ = v • f ′ = 20 meter/second. In terms of the outside clock, that is of the person watching the video, the cart will now hit the ground after t/ f ′ = 0.225 seconds. This makes sense: the video is running twice as fast, the event of interest will happen in half the time. But, what of the horizontal distance the cart will travel after rolling off the table ? The speeding up of the video does not matter to this, as the cart is not actually traveling faster, and it will still cover a distance of d = v•t = 4.5 meters. Notice that this scenario creates a clean mapping between 'when' judgements (time to fall) and expected changes in frame-rate, while 'where' judgements should not be affected by changes in frame rate. This clean separation is not a generally true feature for randomly selected dynamic stimuli judgements, and is the reason we chose the stimuli we did.

With the motivating example of the cart in mind, what would a mental simulation account predict will happen, as people are asked to continue the motion of the cart past the edge of the table, in their imagination?

We considered four distinct models (see Fig. 2): (1) Full: According to this model, people do notice and take into account the change in reference frame, and also take into account the resulting change in content speed. This model calculates an estimation of the change in frame rate f ′ , and uses it to adjust the perceived velocity v ′ , and the timing of events t/ f ′ . Such a model could successfully predict timing and distance judgements in the example above. (2) Null: According to this model, people do not take into account the change in reference frame. Whatever events they observe are taken to be happening in real time. For this model, f ′ = f = 1, and therefore the estimated velocity of things in a scene is simply the observed velocity.

Such a model would not correctly predict when or where events occur in our stimuli. (3) Reference-Frame-Only: According to this model, people do notice and take into account changes in the reference-frame speed like the Full model, but do not apply the required change to the perceived velocity. To put this in plain terms, such a model is equivalent to a person perceiving (or imagining) a sped-up video and recognizing that the video is sped up, correctly anticipating some events will happen earlier as a result (for an external clock), but not then going the extra mental step of realizing that if the video is sped up, the content velocity must be slower than what they are seeing or imagining. In our running example of the toy cart, such a model could correctly predict changes to ground truth timing, but not distance. (4) Content-Speed-Only: According to this model, people do notice and adjust for changes in content speed, but they do not or cannot apply these likely a priori. It would be equivalent to a person who recognizes a toy-cart video is sped up, correctly infers 172 the cart must be moving slower in terms of its original clock, but fails to recognize that events should be 173 taking place faster relative to an external clock, treating f ′ = f = 1 like the Null model. Such a model could 174 correctly predict changes to ground truth distance but not timing, in our running example. 175 0.5× Velocity corrected Time corrected Velocity not corrected Time not corrected Full Null Reference-Frame Only Content-Speed Only

Figure 2. Possible models of mental simulation when changing an imagined scene's reference frame, applied to a specific case. Consider seeing a cart rolling to the edge of a table and being asked to continue its motion in the imagination, when the scene is playing at different frame rates. The Full model suggests people take into account that the entire scene is being sped up or slowed down, and correct for this in judging when the cart will hit the ground relative to an external clock, adjusting the perceived velocity accordingly. The Reference-Frame-Only model suggests people take into account that the entire scene is being sped up or slowed down and so have accurate timing judgements, but do not correct the perceived velocity, such that frame-rate changes will influence final position. The Content-Speed-Only model suggests people correct the perceived velocity, but do not adjust their timing judgements. The Null model suggests people mentally continue the scene without any correction, taking e.g. a sped-up video to indicate a regular video in which the cart is simply moving faster.

in double time ( f ′ = 2 • f ) and generally understands the video is sped up, but mistakenly believes the video is not quite as sped up as it actually is (e.g. the person thinks f ′ = 1.8 • f ). Or, consider a person who watches a video playing at a standard frame rate, in which a cart moves at a speed of 3 m/s, but the person incorrectly perceives the cart as moving at 3.1 m/s. Such errors in perception can lead to deviations from ground truth in a way that is not of interest to our current research. To account for these possible errors, we adjusted model outputs to be in line with human data, in the following two ways: (i) Reference-frame speed was adjusted according to the empirical relationship between playback speed and participant timing judgements. In other words, we use participants' own sensitivity to playback speed in 'when' judgements to allow for human misperception of frame-rate, such as a person that sees a video playing in double-time inaccurately thinking the adjusted frame-rate is 1.8 instead of 2.0; (ii) Content speed was adjusted according to the relationship between ground-truth content speed and participants' position estimation in the baseline conditions showing stimuli happening at regular frame rate (1×). We emphasize this content-speed adjustment was estimated only from 1× trials, and then applied to non-1× trials. This adjustment accounts for the potential perceptual errors, such as a person observing an object that is truly moving at 3 m/s, but perceiving it as moving at 3.1 m/s. These two empirical adjustments were fixed by the data and applied equally to all models, so that any remaining difference between the model results would be due to the workings of the models themselves.

(For analysis on unadjusted models, see the Supplementary Information).

To summarize, we devised four distinct mental simulation models, which align with four different proposals for how people might imagine an entire mental scene as happening faster or slower. These models make different predictions for how and when people deviate from ground truth judgements of when and where events take place. The Full model suggests people can speed up or slow down their mental simulations, and adjust the content of simulations accordingly. The Null model suggests that people cannot speed up or slow things down in the imagination, and that the frame rate for the imagined scene is treated as equal to the external clock. The Reference-Frame-Only model suggests that people can adjust the timing of a mental simulation, but do not adjust the content correctly as a result. The Content-Speed-Only model suggests that people can adjust the content of a mental simulation to account for sped-up or slowed-down scenes, but they do not adjust the frame-rate of the simulation.

We first examined how people continue the motion of a simple entity in their mind's eye, when the scene is presented as taking place either in standard time, or slowed down, or sped up. Study 1 consisted of two different experiments. In both experiments, participants viewed simple animations of a two-dimensional cart, moving horizontally towards the edge of a cliff (see Fig. 3). The animations stopped just as the cart reached the edge of the cliff, and participants were asked to imagine the continued motion of the cart.

Each animation was presented within a square canvas of 1280 × 1280 pixels. We independently manipulated the cart's content speed (200, 250, or 300 pixels per second), the height of the cliff (384 or 895 pixels), and six playback speeds (0.5×, 0.75×, 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 2×). We conveyed the playback speed of each animation in several ways, including both explicit-fixed cues and perceptual-dynamic cues: the rate itself was displayed at the top-left corner of the scene; a timer in the top-right corner showed the "internal The participants in both experiments described in this section saw the same animations of a cart rolling towards the edge of a cliff, and were all asked to continue the animations in their mind. However, participants in the two experiments were given different instructions of how to react. In the "When" Experiment (Experiment 1a), participants were asked to continue the animation in their mind, and press a key at the moment when the cart would have hit the ground, had the animation continued. The duration between the animation freezing and a participant key press was logged as the estimated falling duration. In the "Where"

Experiment (Experiment 1b), a different group of participants was asked to continue the animation in their mind and click on the screen, at the location where the cart would have landed, had the animation continued.

The horizontal distance between a participant's click and the bottom of the cliff was logged as the estimated travel distance.

As explained earlier, we chose projectile motion because it provides a natural dissociation between reference-frame speed and content speed: Given the same cliff height, changing the speed of the cart as it moves horizontally along the plateau changes where the cart will land after it flies off the cliff, but not when it lands. Conversely, changing the playback speed of the video itself changes the landing time (relative to an external clock), but not the location of where the cart ends up. Therefore, participants' estimated timing judgement provides a measure of participants' represented reference-frame speed, and their estimation of the landing position of the cart is a measure of their content speed representation.

We recruited 40 participants from Prolific for each experiment, and applied pre-registered exclusion criteria to them. In the "When" Experiment, 3 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials; 2 participants failed to submit a complete dataset to our server; and 14 additional invalid trials were excluded, leaving 35 participants (21 female, 14 male; age: M = 44.8, SD = 12.1, range = 25-67) and 2506 trials for analysis. In the "Where" Experiment, 2 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials; 1 participant failed to submit a complete dataset to our server; and 9 additional invalid trials were excluded, leaving 37 participants (20 female, 17 male; age: M = 41.1, SD = 12.2, range = 18-72) and 2655 trials for analysis.

Participants in the "when" experiment showed a sensitivity to changes in playback speed (the faster the playback, the sooner they thought the cart will hit the ground), generally in line with models that adjust for frame-rate in mental simulation, and not in line with those that do not. However, participants in the "where" experiment show a sensitivity to playback speed even when taking temporal differences into account, closest to either the Reference-Frame or Null models. Cutting across the experiments, participant behavior is best explained as their mental simulation being sensitive to changes in frame-rate, but not fully correcting for this in the resulting properties of the content of imagined scenes.

This can reflect that participants are not ideally sensitive to manipulations in the ground truth, and is accounted for in model adjustment (see earlier section).

We then examined which mental simulation models can account for this relationship. Both the Full and Reference-Frame-Only (RF-Only) models show a significant correlation between the log estimated falling duration and the log playback speed (Full: β = -0.76, SE = 0.023, t = -32.35, p < 0.0001; RF-Only: β = -0.76, SE = 0.023, t = -32.35, p < 0.0001). These two models make very similar predictions about participants' timing judgement, which is expected, as both of them take the playback speed into account. In contrast to these two models, the Null and Content-Speed-Only (CS-Only) models do not show a significant correlation between the log estimated falling duration and the log playback speed (Null: β = 0.0056, SE = 0.020, t = 0.28, p = 0.78; CS-Only: β = 0.0056, SE = 0.020, t = 0.283, p = 0.777). Again, these two models give similar results, because both of them assume no adjustment to the frame-rate of mental scenes. Overall, our results suggest that participants are taking into account the distortion in reference frame rate when unfolding the adjusted scene in their mind, independent of the content speed, and both the Full and RF-Only models predict the timing judgement of participants. In the following "Where" experiment, we examined participants' content speed representation and investigated how our mind adjusts it according to the reference-frame speed distortion.

2.1.2 Experiment 1b ("Where")

We first examined participants' distance estimation in the 1× videos. A linear mixed-effect model showed a significant relationship between the estimated travel distance and its ground truth (β = 0.48, SE = 0.048, t = 9.98, p < 0.0001). This result suggests that participants are sensitive to the variation in carts' speed in the original video, such that the faster the cart moves, the further along the horizontal axis participants believe it will land. This is not surprising, but is important to establish.

We next analyzed how the playback speed influences the position estimate of participants. Recall that in an ideal simulation, total distances traveled should not be correlated with the speed of the simulation itself (running a video faster does not make the cart in the video go further). However, if mental simulation is affected by the playback speed, we should expect to see that the predicted distance will be of the form:

Where d ′ is the predicted horizontal distance, t is the time it takes the cart to reach the ground in the baseline 1× condition, v is the velocity in baseline 1× condition, and f ′ is the new frame-rate relative to baseline.

To express this multiplicative relationship as a linear one, the variables can be log-transformed:

We fitted a mixed-effect model predicting participants' log(d ′ ) with log(t), log(v) and log( f ′ ). It showed a significant relationship between the log estimated travel distance, and the log playback speed (β = 0.31, SE = 0.013, t = 24.15, p < 0.0001, and see Fig. 4). Furthermore, after the playback speed adjustment, all the models showed a significant correlation between the log estimated distance and the log playback speed (Null: β = 0.42, SE = 0.020, t = 20.91, p < 0.0001; RF-Only: β =0.42, SE = 0.018, t = 23.37, p < 0.0001; Full: β = 0.096, SE = 0.016, t = 5.82, p < 0.0001; CS-only: β = 0.10, SE = 0.020, t = 5.13, p < 0.0001). This is expected, because all the models were adjusted based on participants' playback speed estimation.

As shown in Experiment 1a, participants overestimate the low playback speed, and underestimate the high ones. So, recovering the content speed as v = v ′ f ′ leads them to underestimate the speed at low playback speeds and overestimate the speed at high playback. As a mid-point summary, the "where" experiment shows that participants' judgments of content properties were affected by frame-rate changes. The specific performance does not fall within any of the models, but is closer to the Reference-frame-only or Null models. It suggests that the mind can discount some, but not all of the changes to the frame-rate of the mental scene when recovering the content speed.

Considering both experiments together: The results of our "When" experiment suggest that participants were generally sensitive to the manipulation of reference-frame speed, and adjusted their mental simulation to take place faster or slower as a whole. This speaks against the Null and Content-Speed-Only models. Our "Where" experiment findings show that participants can partially adjust the properties of mental simulation following the change in temporal reference frame, but not fully, with their performance falling between the Reference-Frame-Only and Full model. In other words: When speeding up the mental scene, participants seemed to imagine the objects inside the scene as actually moving faster, though to a lesser extent than the direct increase in perceived motion.

Our use of simple animated scenes was an intentional choice, meant to help isolate extraneous factors and features. But, it leaves open the possibility that people change content properties differently when given realistic motion cues. To examine this, we conducted additional experiments that kept the logic of Study 1, but used realistic scenes.

3 Study 2: "When" and "Where" Task with realistic balls Our next set of studies repeated the general logic, methods, and procedure of Study 1. However, instead of watching simplified animated stimuli, participants were shown videos of real scenes. In the videos, a person waved at the camera, and then pushed a green yoga ball off a stadium balconyfoot_1 . The video was clipped at the moment when the ball reached the edge of the ledge, and participants were asked to continue its motion in their mind (see Fig. 5). As before, one group of participants was recruited to judge when the ball would hit the ground (Experiment 2a), and another to judge where it would land (Experiment 2b).

We included 6 different videos, each showing the ball rolling at different speeds. On top of this, there were 6 different playback speeds: 0.5×, 0.75×, 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 2×. Also, each trial randomly displayed the video either in its original form, or mirrored horizontally.

We recruited 80 participants online via Prolific (40 for each experiment). Each participant completed 350 36 trials. We then applied our pre-registered exclusion criteria. In the "When" Experiment, no participants 351 were excluded, and 6 invalid trials were dropped 2 . This left 40 participants (21 female, 19 male; age: M = 40.4, SD = 12.6, range = 21-69) and 1434 trials for analysis. In the "Where" Experiment, 3 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials, and 3 additional invalid trials were dropped, leaving 37 participants (26 female, 11 male); age: M = 50.3, SD = 13.4, range = 28-77) and 1329 trials analyzed. The ground truth horizontal velocity, and the timing of the ball hitting the ground was determined by having two of the authors independently annotate the videos. The two annotations matched closely, with Pearson's r = 0.996 (mean difference of 3.75 pixels per second) for horizontal velocity and r = 0.997 (mean difference of 0.011 second) for ground timing.

3.1 Results

3.1.1 Experiment 2a ("When")

We repeated the analysis logic of Experiment 1a. A generalized linear mixed-effect model showed a significant negative correlation between the estimated log falling duration and the log playback speed (β = -0.76, SE = 0.020, t = -36.99, p < 0.0001), meaning participants were sensitive to the changes in frame-rate. Similar to people, both the Full and RF-Only models showed a significant negative correlation between the log estimated falling duration and the log playback speed (Full model: β = -0.78, SE = 0.020, t = -38.18, p < 0.0001; RF-Only model: β = -0.78, SE = 0.021, t = -36.88, p < 0.0001). By contrast, the Null and CS-only models did not show such a correlation (Null model: β = -0.0099, SE = 0.016, t = -0.62, p = 0.53; CS-only model: β = -0.0099, SE = 0.016, t = -0.62, p = 0.53).

When examining how well the models captured participants' sensitivity to changes in playback speed (see Fig. 5, top), we find the Full and RF-Only models' slope estimations both overlap with human's (Participants: slope = -0.76, CI = [-0.80, -0.72]; Full: slope = -0.78, CI = [-0.82, -0.74] and RF-Only models: slope = -0.78, CI = [-0.82, -0.74]). By contrast, the Null and Content-Speed-Only models did not capture the participant slope (Null: slope = -0.010, CI = [-0.041, 0.021] and Content-Speed-Only models: slope = -0.010, CI = [-0.041, 0.021]). This makes sense, because we adjust the models' sensitivity to playback speed across all models in the same way, according to human data (for more details, see General Methods), but Null and Content-Speed-Only model do not have sensitivity to playback speed by design.

We also used an MSE and correlation analysis to test how each model fits human response. Though MSE did not significantly differ among the models (Full: MSE = 0.17, CI = [0.04, 0.87]; RF-Only: MSE = tially degrading model fit. As with Experiment 1a, the results are in line with both the Full model and the Reference-Frame-Only model (and not with Null or the Content-Speed-Only model). This suggests people are aware of the distortion in reference frame, and imagine the whole scene as sped up or slowed down when considering what happens next.

3.1.2 Experiment 2b ("Where")

We first examined whether participants were sensitive to variation in the object speed in 1× videos. A linear mixed-effect model showed a significant relationship between the estimated travel distance and its ground truth (β = 0.20, SE = 0.044, t = 4.65, p < 0.0001). The slope of 0.20 suggests that participants do indeed see faster or slower balls as moving faster or slower (a trivial but important baseline to establish), but also that their perception of the ball speed is not 1:1 with ground truth. As mentioned in the General Methods, such perceptual or representational errors are expected, and accounted for in model adjustment in the same way across models.

We next analyzed how the playback speed influences "where" judgements. Another mixed-effect model showed a significant relationship between the log estimated travel distance and the log playback speed (β = 0.12, SE = 0.012, t = 9.73, p < 0.0001). After adjustment, all models showed a significant correlation between the estimated position and the playback speed (Full: β = 0.081, SE = 0.012, t = 6.92, p < 0.0001; Content-Speed-Only: β = 0.075, SE = 0.016, t = 4.67, p < 0.0001; RF-Only: β = 0.39, SE = 0.013, t = 30.73, p < 0.0001; Null: β = 0.39, SE = 0.016, t = 24.37, p < 0.0001).

We then evaluated which model fits human data best (see Fig. 5 To summarize the results: As with Experiment 1a, participants seemed to imagine the scenes as a whole as sped up or slowed down. However, when taking into account both the 'where' and 'when' responses, the overall pattern of results is best explained by the Full model. So, participants seem to correctly account for the changes in temporal reference frame, by adjusting the content of imagined scenes. As the only difference in presentation compared to Study 1 was the use of realistic scenes, the interim conclusion would be that people's failure to fully adjust content properties of Experiment 1b was due to the lack of familiar/realistic motion cues.

While we varied our experiments so far in terms of content speed, temporal frame-rate, participant response, and realism of the scenes, they all focused on one kind of motion (projectile motion following horizontal launching). To better establish the generality of the findings to other types of realistic motion, we next moved from projectile to pendulum motion.

4 Study 3: "When" and "Where" Task with realistic pendulums Study 1 and 2 considered how people represent and simulate projectile motion across changes to the temporal reference frame. We used stimuli that depicted projectile motion (following horizontal launching) because it cleanly mapped different parts of motion to changes in content or reference-frame speeds. We next examined people's behavior when presented with a different kind of stimuli, which showed pendulum motion. We chose this type of stimuli as it also dissociates between reference-frame and content speed: Given the same rope length, changing a pendulum's angular velocity (scene content) will change where the pendulum reaches its highest point, but not the pendulum's period; changing the frame-rate of the scene as a whole (temporal reference frame) will change only the pendulum's period, not where it ends up at its apex.

We note that the known separation between pendulum period and angular speed is obtained by using approximations that assume small angle differences. In real life, the period increases slightly with the increase in the pendulum's speed. However, this does not confound our analysis here: If participants represent the content and reference-frame speed separately, then the period should decrease when the entire scene is sped increase with the increase in the playback speed. with video clips that showed a person pushing a bag tied to a rope, played at various playback speeds (see Fig. 6). The videos ended mid-motion, when the bag reached the lowest point in its arc.
