4.1 Results

4.1.1 Experiment 3a ("When")

Like the projectile motion case, the swinging time of a pendulum has a multiplicative relationship with the playback speed: where t ′ is the swinging time after the playback speed manipulation, t is the swinging time in the 1× original video, and f ′ is the playback speed when we fix the original frame-rate arbitrarily to be f = 1.

Again, this is simply a way of saying that if the video is playing back at (say) double speed, then the pendulum will reach its apex in half the time, by the measure of an external clock. We again log-transformed all the variables to obtain a linear relationship:

We used a generalized linear mixed-effect model predicting the log(t ′ ) with fixed effects log(t) and log( f ′ ) and participants as random effects. We found a significant negative relationship between the log estimated swinging duration and the log playback speed (β = -0.50, SE = 0.023, t = -21.77, p < 0.0001). We then examined which mental simulation model could account for this relationship (see Fig. 6, top). As in Experiment 1a and 2a, we found that the Full and RF-Only model showed a significant negative relationship between the log estimated swinging duration and the log playback speed (Full model: β = -0.45, SE = 0.023, The pattern of results we found in Experiment 3a was similar to that of both Experiments 1a and 2a, in line with the Full and the Reference-Frame-Only models. The repeating conclusion is that the data suggest that participants are indeed able to take into account the distortion in reference-frame rate when imagining how mental scenes unfold, independent of the content speed.

4.1.2 Experiment 3b ("Where")

In an ideal simulation, the swinging angle of a pendulum does not correlate with the playback speed (just as the distance traveled by an object doesn't change when a video is slowed down or sped up). However, for a model that simulates the unfolding of a scene directly using the perceived angular speed, the swinging angle would be: where θ ′ is the swinging angle after playback speed manipulation, ω is the angular speed of the pendulum at the bottom in the original 1× video, f ′ is the new frame-rate relative to baseline, L is the rope length and g is the gravitational acceleration.

Since both L and g are constant, the √︂ L g term is simply some constant. We again log-transformed all the variables to obtain a linear relationship: where c is a constant.

We first examined whether participants were sensitive to the variation in pendulum speed in 1× videos.

A linear mixed-effect model showed a significant relationship between the estimated swinging angle and its ground truth (β = 0.45, SE = 0.030, t = 14.99, p < 0.0001). This is, again, a simple but important baseline to establish. It shows that participants see pendulums that are swinging faster (or slower) as indeed swinging faster (or slower), and think they will reach higher (or lower). It also shows the relationship between ground truth and participant perception isn't 1:1. But, again, this error in estimation is not important for our investigation here, and it is adjusted for in the same way across all the models.

We next analyzed how the playback speed influenced participants' angle responses. Another mixedeffect model showed a significant positive relationship between the estimated swinging angle and the playback speed (β = 0.047 , SE = 0.013, t = 3.66, p = 0.00026). All of the models showed a similar significant correlation (Full: β = 0.29, SE = 0.017, t = 17.21, p < 0.0001; Content-Speed-Only: β = 0.28, SE = 0.018, t = 15.13, p < 0.0001; RF-Only: β = 0.54, SE = 0.017, t = 32.08, p < 0.0001; Null: β = 0.53, SE = 0.020, t = 25.75, p < 0.0001). See Fig. 6, bottom.

We also evaluated each model by analyzing None of the models perfectly matched the log(θ ′ ) ∼ log( f ′ ) slope of participant response (Participants: slope = 0.0471, CI = [0.022, 0.072]; Full: slope = 0.285, CI = [0.253, 0.318]; Content-Speed-Only: slope = 0.28, CI = [0.24, 0.31]; RF-Only: slope = 0.54, CI = [0.50, 0.57]; Null: slope = 0.53, CI = [0.49, 0.57]). The slope shown by participants is significantly smaller than predicted by any of the models, though the Full and Content-Speed-Only models have a closer fit to the data than the Null and RF-Only models.

The flatter slope shows that participant response is very consistent across the playback speed, even when their playback speed estimation is not as accurate. One potential explanation is that participants use cues other than the direct perceived angular velocity and playback speed to estimate the actual moving speed of the pendulum. For example, participants might infer how vigorous the push was by observing the person's movement, and use it as an additional feature to adjust their estimation of the actual angular speed of the bag at the point at which the video paused.

The overall pattern of results we found in Experiment 3b was in line with Experiment 2b (and, as a result, counter to Experiment 1b). The pattern is closest to the Full model. Taken together with the results of Experiment 3a, the analysis suggests that participants (i) do understand a sped-up or slowed-down video is different in terms of its temporal reference frame, (ii) use the altered reference frame when imagining what takes place next, and (iii) can adjust the content of an imagined scene accordingly. As with Study 2, the results of Study 3 suggest that people's apparent incorrect adjustment to content speed in simplified stimuli (Study 1) was due to a lack of realistic/familiar motion cues.

5 General Discussion

A mental scene has its contents: imagining a porcelain cup sliding along on a slippery table towards a slab of concrete is not the same as imagining a garbage truck sliding on ice. The contents of a mental scene have their properties, and those have consequences: imagining a cup sliding after a gentle push will end differently than imagining that cup traveling at great speed. This is all quite obvious so far. But, a mental scene also has its reference frames: do you see the cup sliding from the point of view of the person who pushed it, or from the point of view of the cup? Much of the research on mental simulation has studied the content of imagined scenes, and nearly all the work on reference frames has studied changes in spatial frames and perspective. Here, we examined a different basic component of reference in the imaginationthe rate at which a mental scene moves.

In principle, the content of a mental scene is independent of its reference frames. Speeding up a video of a porcelain cup hitting concrete will not make the shards fly any farther. But for the human mind, content and the temporal reference frame may be linked. Imagining the entire scene of the unfortunate porcelain cup speeding up might indeed make the shards fly farther in the mind. Here, we asked: does the mind represent changes in the temporal reference frame independent of the content of imagined scenes, and does it adjust mental simulations accordingly?

We investigated how people imagine the simple motion of objects, when asked to speed up or slow down the imagined scene as a whole. Specifically, we showed people projectile motion and pendulum motion at different frame rates, and then asked them to continue the events in their mind's eye, and judge when and where certain events took place. The use of this type of motion lets us dissociate reference-frame speed and content speed, by mapping them separately onto judgements of timing and position. We used stylized animations, and realistic videos. Across three studies and six experiments, we found that: (i) People were generally able to adjust the playback speed of their mental simulation for all scenes. Carts and balls in slow motion fell slower to the ground in the mind's eye, pendulums in half-time swung slower. (ii) People could recover and adjust imagined content separately from reference frame. However, for stylized animations, people did not adjust the content fully. People's results for stylized animations were best explained by a

Reference-Frame-Only mental simulation model, and their results for realistic scenes were best explained by a Full mental simulation model.

The results and models suggest that people can in principle separate imagined content and temporal reference frame, but this separation did not happen fully for stylized animations. When considered from the perspective of a limited mental game engine account 2,3 , the following might be taking place: In order to unfold an imagined scene step by step, a mental simulation needs to fix the initial properties of entities (including their velocity V ), and the frame-rate of the simulation as a whole, F. In our experiments, both V and F were informed by perception. On this view, perception is handing off to simulation the input that the frame-rate appears to be f ′ , and the velocity appears to be v. But it is a separate mental operation to then adjust v to account for f ′ . Realistic motion cues may directly affect the apparent v that is being handed off.

Our current studies open up many directions for future exploration in studying the effects of temporal rate distortion on the contents of mental simulation and the imagination. We next consider a few of the important ones. First, while we studied how speeding up or slowing down mental simulation might distort the speed of objects in the imagination, other properties may change in different ways. More particularly, the read-out of mental-simulation may be distorted in different ways than the input that controls its next step.

To put this distinction in terms of a mental game engine framework: properties that determine the initial setup of the mental simulation (or propel it forward via a step-by-step transition function) may be differently affected by frame-rate changes than the modules that take the image-based output of mental simulation as their input, and such downstream modules are likely shared by both perception and imagination. To give some examples of how these may play out differently: try to imagine an open palm moving at great speed but in slow motion directly towards a face. You may see the moment of contact of the palm with the face, the ripples on the cheeks of the person being hit, and their slow and anguished turning away from the palm.

You may correctly judge that such a strike is painful, but even so you may lack the implicit perception of the striking force that accompanies such a scene playing in real time. Compare this also to imagining a hand striking a face in double time. Such a slap might 'feel' even more forceful than it is if seen in real time.

Moving beyond simple physical properties, higher-level inferences that are downstream of imagined scenes may be affected by mental speed-up and slow-down. In direct perception, sped-up and slowed-down videos are known to affect higher-level judgements, from aesthetics 35 and intentionality 36, 37 , to luxury 38 , which suggests that imagined scenes may be affected in similar ways.

Beyond testing the distortion of additional properties, another direction to explore would be temporal distortions that are entirely self-generated, as opposed to a continuation of perceptual scenes. In our studies, we had participants view videos and then asked them to continue those events in their mind's eye. However, people can also imagine things happening in a slowed down or sped up way without direct perceptual input (we asked the reader to do so throughout this paper). This route would bypass the direct input of perception, and may lead to different content adjustments. However, we caution that while it is easy enough simply to ask people to imagine things happening faster or slower, it is experimentally difficult to determine how people then continue things in the imagination given such instructions. While previous studies on mental transformations (such as scanning or rotation) could rely on a standard and consistent notion of an internal clock to draw conclusions about the speed of mental simulation, in our suggested manipulations both content and frame-rate can vary and are coupled. This makes it challenging for the experimenter to separately determine both of these changes, without starting from some agreed on perceptual input (as in our stimuli). We have not resolved this issue ourselves, and leave it as a challenge for further research.

A third important direction for future research would examine the degree to which speeding up and slowing down an entire imagined scene takes a toll on mental resources. While an ideal, limitless simulation can run things at whatever frame-rate desired, in practice changes to frame-rate come with a cost. To the degree that filling in the details of a specific moment in an imagined scene takes time, moving faster between frames will reduce the level of details available at each frame, predicting a loss of imagery-related detail (though the distinction between physical-spatial reasoning and graphical rendering 39 may affect loss of spatial vs. graphical detail differently). Conversely, imagining things in slow-motion may allow for greater filling in of detail, but tax memory resources as a result.

The ability to speed up and slow down animations and videos is a recent invention in human history. In asking the reader to imagine things as happening faster or slower, we have relied on the implicit assumption that they are familiar with relevant examples from daily life. Our experiments were with adult participants based in the US, and similarly have an implicit assumption of familiarity of sped-up and slowed-down events. The fact that participants could generally adjust for temporal frame-rate and content properties suggests they understood the manipulation and backs up this implicit assumption. But, it is possible that notions of speeding up or slowing down scenes in the imagination make no sense to someone unfamiliar with relevant technology. We accept this as a limitation of the current research, and cross-cultural and developmental studies are necessary to establish the generality of the findings. But, we would also note that for spatial reference, surveys on memory that predate film and television found that people spontaneously recall or imagine a scene from a third-person perspective 40 , despite having no experience with being outside of their bodies, or observing the relevant technique in films. This suggests that at least in principle, some reference changes in the imagination are possible without direct experience of the changes. In addition, old tales of whole lifetimes unfolding in the imagination while mere moments pass in real life (such as Shen Jiji's "The World Inside a Pillow") and pre-modern academic discussions of internal time as separate from external time 41 also suggestively point to a basic cognitive distinction between internal and external timing (though we emphasize they do not directly line up with the notion of the imagined things themselves being represented as taking place faster or slower to the mental observer). Again, further cross-cultural work and developmental work is needed to examine and establish the generality of the findings.

The imagination can feel like it is conjuring up a play inside our heads. But we must distinguish the stage directions from the set and players. People may call to mind different players, and have them read different lines, or move the audience to different perspectives. Here, we explored a different kind of direction: running the whole scene fast or slow. We found that for realistic scenes, people can do this, while keeping a separation between the tempo and the players. For stylized scenes, the change in imagined time bled into the imagined scenes. But whatever the pace, eventually it's curtains.

Figure1. Changing the content or reference frame of scenes. (a) An example of an everyday scene unfolding at normal playback speed (1×). One could either change the content speed, e.g. making the player and ball genuinely move faster, so that the ball travels farther in the same scene time. Or, one could change the reference-frame speed, e.g. making the whole scene play at 2×, so events occur sooner relative to an external clock, but object velocities are unchanged. (b) The paradigm we used in our studies dissociate content properties and reference frame by using motion types that map changes in either content or reference frame to different judgements. Here, we show the example of projectile motion, specifically a cart rolling off a cliff. Increasing the horizontal cart speed will make it fall further, but not change its vertical speed, and so not change the time to impact. Making the entire scene run faster will make the cart hit the ground sooner (relative to an external clock), but not change where it ends up. So, having participants judge 'where' the cart ended up and 'when' it hit the ground allows us to work backwards to how they reason when speeding up or slowing down a mental scene.

Participants were asked to continue the motion of the cart in their mind, and either answer when it hit the ground (Experiment 1a) or where it landed (Experiment 1b). Participants in the "when" experiment showed a sensitivity to changes in playback speed (the faster the playback, the sooner they thought the cart will hit the ground), generally in line with models that adjust for frame-rate in mental simulation, and not in line with those that do not. However, participants in the "where" experiment show a sensitivity to playback speed even when taking temporal differences into account, closest to either the Reference-Frame or Null models. Cutting across the experiments, participant behavior is best explained as their mental simulation being sensitive to changes in frame-rate, but not fully correcting for this in the resulting properties of the content of imagined scenes.
